papers.title: A serendipitous CMOS quantum sensor
papers.summary: Nature Electronics, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41928-026-01735-9 Titanium nitride films native to a commercial complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) process can become high-impedance superconductors at millikelvin temperatures, providing compact, sensitive readout of semiconductor spin qubits from within a chip’s existing gate metallization.

papers.title: Hall-Density Collapse as Direct Evidence for Percolative Conduction Onset in Monolayer MoS$_2$ Transistors
authors: C. J. L. de la Rosa
papers.summary: The origin of the apparent metal-insulator transition in two-dimensional electron systems remains debated. Using temperature-dependent transport and Hall measurements on industry-relevant MoS$_2$ monolayer FETs with amorphous HfO$_2$ dielectrics, we establish classical percolation as the underlying mechanism. We report two complementary signatures of disorder-driven conduction onset: a temperature-independent Hall-density collapse as a function of absolute gate voltage and a vanishing activation energy at a characteristic carrier density $n_{\mathrm{c}}$, identified as the percolation threshold. These findings identify dielectric-interface disorder, rather than channel quality alone, as the key parameter governing device turn-on. The extracted activation barriers reach values substantially exceeding room-temperature thermal energies, indicating that disorder-driven conduction onset remains relevant well beyond cryogenic transport.

papers.title: Atomic-Scale Phonon Engineering for Enhanced Thermal Transport in Wafer-Scale-Bonded $β$-Ga$_{2}$O$_{3}$/SiC Heterostructures
papers.summary: Bonding semiconductors to substrates with high thermal conductivity is a promising way to solve the heat-dissipation problem of materials that transport heat poorly, and it avoids the lattice-matching constraints of conventional epitaxy. However, the lattice mismatch remains, leaving the two materials with mismatched phonon states, while poor interface quality scatters phonons even more. Together, these effects block phonon transport across the bonded interface and make interfacial thermal resistance a critical bottleneck, calling for careful interface engineering. Here, $β$-Ga$_{2}$O$_{3}$/SiC serves as a model system for a phonon-bridging strategy. A nanoscale crystalline Si interlayer is designed and fabricated by wafer bonding to bridge the mismatched phonon states of $β$-Ga$_{2}$O$_{3}$ and SiC. Spatially resolved electron energy-loss spectroscopy and molecular dynamics simulations show that this Si layer opens new channels for phonon transport across the interface. The engineered interface raises the interfacial thermal conductance to 165 MW m$^{-2}$ K$^{-1}$ -- the highest value yet reported for $β$-Ga$_{2}$O$_{3}$/SiC interfaces. These results offer an effective way to manage heat in $β$-Ga$_{2}$O$_{3}$ devices and point to a general approach for building phonon-bridging interfaces that improve heat dissipation in heterogeneous systems.

papers.title: An opto-electrically decoupled phototransistor for solar-blind ultraviolet detection
papers.summary: Solar-blind ultraviolet (UV) photodetectors have been primarily developed using ultrawide-bandgap (UWBG) semiconductors, where the wide bandgap enables low dark current and intrinsic solar-blind selectivity. However, the same wide-bandgap nature limits carrier modulation, particularly doping control and junction engineering, imposing fundamental challenges for high-sensitivity detection and scalable integration. Here, we demonstrate an opto-electrically decoupled solar-blind UV phototransistor by integrating a perovskite p–n photovoltage generator with a carbon nanotube (CNT) field-effect transistor. This architecture separates photon conversion from carrier transport, where the perovskite heterojunction generates a photovoltage that electrostatically modulates the CNT channel without interfacial carrier transfer. Under 265 nm illumination, the device achieves a responsivity of 2908 A W−1, a specific detectivity of 1.6 × 1013 Jones, and rise/decay times of 5.6/15.5 ms. The low-temperature fabrication process is compatible with silicon back-end-of-line integration, providing a route toward highly integrated solar-blind UV sensing with front-end bandpass filtering, beyond conventional UWBG semiconductor systems.

papers.title: Atomistic understanding of hybrid bonding in Cu interfaces using multiscale microscopy
papers.summary: Achieving wafer-scale reliability in Cu–Cu hybrid bonding remains challenging due to process-induced non-uniformities and the limited understanding of buried interfacial contamination. Here, we employ a correlative multiscale microscopy framework combining scanning electron microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom probe tomography (APT) to investigate bond degradation from the wafer center to the edge. We observe progressive bond deterioration characterized by interfacial delamination, reduced Cu grain size, and the formation of a nanometer-scale amorphous interlayer. While such interlayers have been widely observed in hybrid bonding, their chemical nature has remained largely unresolved. APT directly reveals that the interlayer consists of Si-, C-, and N-bearing species consistent with contributions from the adjacent SiCN dielectric, together with Cu oxide and organic-related contaminants. By correlating interlayer chemistry and thickness with microstructural evolution, we establish a direct link between interfacial contamination, suppressed cross-interface grain growth, and bond degradation. Furthermore, we observe a progressive thickness-dependent degradation, where interfacial thickening from ∼1 to 2 nm at the center to ∼2 to 3 nm in the donut region is accompanied by deterioration in mechanical bond integrity and localized delamination. These findings provide atomistic insight into the chemistry governing hybrid bond reliability and establish quantitative guidelines for process optimization toward wafer-scale integration.

papers.title: Experimental demonstration of dual-polarization nonreciprocal thermal emission at moderate magnetic fields
papers.summary: Conventional thermal emitters obey Kirchhoff's law of thermal radiation, which requires emissivity and absorptivity to be equal at each wavelength, angle, and polarization. This in turn places a fundamental limit on a range of radiative energy technologies as well as heat transfer. This constraint can however be overcome using magneto-optic semiconductors, which break Lorentz reciprocity under an applied magnetic field. However, in most prior experimental demonstrations, nonreciprocity has been restricted to TM polarization, since the electric field of TE-polarized light is parallel to the applied magnetic field. Here, we experimentally demonstrate nonreciprocal absorption in both polarizations at the same wavelengths and angles from a single structure, wherein a germanium Mie-resonant metasurface on a doped InAs layer scatters TE-polarized light into near fields with components perpendicular to the magnetic field, allowing the magneto-optic response of the InAs to act on them. Under a 0.48 T field from a permanent Halbach array, this structure exhibits a difference in absorptivity between $+B$ and $-B$ of 0.035 in both TE and TM polarization at 16.6 $μ$m. Our approach shows that the magneto-optic response of a planar semiconductor and the resonances of a dielectric metasurface can be designed together, offering a potential route to dual-polarization nonreciprocity at fields available from permanent magnets for emerging energy and heat transfer technologies.

papers.title: A Design Rule for Passive Reconfigurable Microwave Devices
papers.summary: Every reconfigurable microwave device places a tuning element - a varactor, a diode, transistor, microelectromechanical or phase-change switch, a ferroelectric or liquid-crystal load - inside a fixed passive network. The network can make a small change of the element produce a large change of the response, and design practice often credits it with the device's tuning capability. This paper shows that a fixed, linear, passive network cannot add to that capability. Each tuning element carries a tuning budget, a dimensionless length computed from its own impedance trajectory, and a fixed passive network can transmit that budget or lose part of it, never enlarge it. The unit of the budget is the hyperbolic distance of the Smith chart: the distance from a match is the logarithm of the voltage standing-wave ratio, and the distance between two states sets their mutual mismatch and is the logarithm of their commutation quality factor. From one inequality we derive closed-form, ready-to-use limits for analog and digital phase shifters, true-time-delay lines, switches, attenuators, vector modulators, impedance tuners, tunable filters, reconfigurable antennas, metasurface cells and multiport networks; the two-state and attenuation limits are attained by explicit circuits, and the phase limit by a constant-loss trajectory. We introduce the $Λ$-chart, a Smith-chart companion on which budgets and requirements are read graphically, and apply it to four published microwave case studies.
